options.C: Dispensing restricted pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: Conducting mandatory annual financial audits

explanation: Telephone triage involves evaluating patient symptoms remotely to determine the urgency and appropriate level of healthcare needed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h4)

question: How is tele-nursing applied in maternal and child health within remote settings?

options.A: By tracking pregnancy milestones and counseling mothers virtually
options.B: By replacing all pediatric vaccination clinics with home visits
options.C: By prohibiting mothers from contacting healthcare providers
options.D: By performing routine deliveries via video call alone

explanation: Tele-nursing supports maternal and child health by allowing nurses to track pregnancies, provide counseling, and monitor neonatal development remotely. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h4)

question: Which regulatory body governs professional nursing practice and standards in Nigeria?

options.A: The Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria
options.B: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN)
options.C: The Federal Ministry of Information
options.D: The World Health Organization

explanation: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) establishes the professional scope, licensing rules, and ethical standards for Nigerian nurses. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h5)

question: Why is data security and encryption critical in tele-nursing practice?

options.A: To ensure patient confidentiality and comply with data protection laws
options.B: To increase internet browsing speeds for video streaming
options.C: To automatically generate nursing care plans
options.D: To eliminate the need for patient informed consent

explanation: Encryption and data security protect sensitive patient health records from unauthorized access and uphold patient confidentiality. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h5)

question: Which of the following is a major advantage of tele-nursing for patients?

options.A: Elimination of all chronic health conditions
options.B: Improved accessibility and reduced travel time/costs
options.C: Guaranteed face-to-face physical examinations daily
options.D: Free smartphones provided to every citizen

explanation: Tele-nursing enhances access to care and saves patients the time and expense associated with traveling to distant health facilities. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h6)

question: What is a prominent barrier to tele-nursing implementation in regions like Nigeria?

options.A: An oversupply of high-speed internet connections
options.B: Erratic power supply and unstable internet connectivity
options.C: Lack of interest from patients needing care
options.D: Excessive physical examination tools in homes

explanation: Unstable internet connectivity and erratic electricity supply pose significant practical challenges for remote healthcare delivery in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h6)

question: What role do emerging technologies like AI play in the future of tele-nursing?

options.A: They completely replace human nurses with robotic administrators
options.B: They assist with predictive symptom analysis and advanced remote monitoring
options.C: They prevent patients from ever needing health education
options.D: They eliminate all legal and ethical nursing regulations

explanation: AI and advanced wearables enhance tele-nursing by supporting predictive symptom analysis and real-time biometric tracking. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h7)

question: What is crucial for the successful expansion of tele-nursing in Nigeria's future?

options.A: Investment in telecommunications infrastructure and rural electrification
options.B: A complete ban on mobile phones in healthcare settings
options.C: The removal of nursing informatics from educational curricula
options.D: Restricting tele-nursing strictly to private urban hospitals

explanation: Expanding tele-nursing in Nigeria requires strong investments in telecommunications infrastructure and reliable power supply. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary function of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED)?

options.A: To provide mechanical chest compressions during cardiac arrest
options.B: To analyze heart rhythms and deliver an electrical shock if a shockable rhythm is detected
options.C: To maintain an open airway in an unresponsive patient
options.D: To monitor continuous arterial blood pressure in emergency settings

explanation: An AED is specifically designed to analyze a patient's heart rhythm and deliver a therapeutic electrical shock when a shockable rhythm like ventricular fibrillation is present. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h1)

question: Approximately what percentage does a victim's survival rate decrease for every minute that passes without defibrillation?

options.A: 1 to 3 percent
options.B: 3 to 5 percent
options.C: 7 to 10 percent
options.D: 15 to 20 percent

explanation: The survival rate for a cardiac arrest victim drops by about 7 to 10 percent for every minute that defibrillation is delayed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h1)

question: What are the core clinical signs that indicate an AED should be used on a patient?

options.A: Chest pain, diaphoresis, and hypertension
options.B: Unresponsiveness, absence of normal breathing, and lack of a pulse
options.C: Tachypnea, fever, and altered mental status
options.D: Bradycardia, hypotension, and pale skin

explanation: An AED is indicated when a patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no pulse, which are the classic signs of sudden cardiac arrest. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h2)

question: Which of the following heart rhythms are considered shockable by an AED?

options.A: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity
options.B: Sinus bradycardia and premature ventricular contractions
options.C: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
options.D: Atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia

explanation: AEDs are specifically programmed to recognize and deliver shocks for ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h2)

question: What is the purpose of pediatric pads or an energy attenuator on an AED?

options.A: To increase the electrical current for pediatric patients
options.B: To reduce the electrical energy dose delivered to children
options.C: To record the ECG reading on paper instead of digitally
options.D: To speed up the rhythm analysis process

explanation: Pediatric pads or an energy attenuation system lower the energy output of the shock to a safe and appropriate level for young children. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h3)

question: Which accessory is typically found in an AED rescue kit to ensure proper pad contact on a hairy chest?

options.A: Antiseptic wipes
options.B: A razor
options.C: A stethoscope
options.D: Medical tape

explanation: A razor is included in the rescue kit so that excessive chest hair can be removed quickly to ensure the electrode pads adhere properly to the skin. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h3)

question: What is the correct standard placement for adult AED electrode pads?

options.A: Both pads placed directly in the center of the chest over the sternum
options.B: One pad on the upper right chest and the other on the lower left rib area
options.C: One pad on the upper left chest and the other on the upper right back
options.D: Both pads placed vertically on the left side of the ribcage

explanation: Adult AED pads are placed on the upper right chest below the collarbone and on the lower left rib area to ensure current travels effectively across the heart. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h4)

question: What action must the rescuer take immediately after the AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Check for a carotid pulse for at least 60 seconds
options.B: Turn off the AED and wait for advanced medical personnel
options.C: Immediately resume high-quality CPR starting with chest compressions
options.D: Remove the electrode pads and wipe the patient's skin

explanation: Rescuers must immediately resume CPR starting with chest compressions following a shock delivery, as directed by standard resuscitation protocols. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary goal regarding 'hands-off time' when integrating an AED with CPR?

options.A: To maximize the time rescuers spend checking for a pulse
options.B: To minimize any interruptions in chest compressions
options.C: To allow the AED battery to recharge between analyses
options.D: To give the physician time to arrive at the bedside

explanation: Minimizing hands-off time means keeping interruptions in chest compressions as brief as possible to maintain adequate blood flow to vital organs. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h5)

question: How long should a single cycle of CPR last between AED rhythm analyses in standard protocols?

options.A: 30 seconds
options.B: 1 minute
options.C: 2 minutes
options.D: 5 minutes

explanation: Rescuers perform CPR for approximately 2 minutes before the AED automatically pauses to re-analyze the patient's heart rhythm. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h5)

question: How should a nurse handle an implanted pacemaker when preparing to apply AED pads?

options.A: Place the AED pad directly over the pacemaker to ensure optimal shock delivery
options.B: Avoid placing the AED pad directly over the device by placing it at least one inch away
options.C: Remove the pacemaker surgically before applying the AED
options.D: Refrain from using the AED entirely if an implanted device is present

explanation: AED pads must not be placed directly over an implanted medical device because it can block energy delivery and damage the unit; pads should be placed at least an inch away. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h6)

question: What is the proper action if medication patches are present on the patient's chest where the AED pad needs to go?

options.A: Leave the patches on and place the pad directly over them
options.B: Remove the patches, wipe the skin clean, and then apply the pad
options.C: Pierce the patches with a needle to drain the medication
options.D: Cover the patches with thick gauze before applying the pad

explanation: Medication patches must be removed and the skin wiped clean before pad placement to prevent skin burns and interference with electrical current transmission. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h6)

question: What should a nurse routinely inspect regarding the electrode pads on an AED unit?

options.A: The color of the outer packaging
options.B: The expiration dates on the pad packaging
options.C: The electrical resistance of the metallic gel
options.D: The brand name of the manufacturing company

explanation: Nurses must regularly inspect the expiration dates on electrode pads because expired pads contain dried gel that compromises adhesion and conductivity. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h7)

question: What indicates that an AED is generally ready for immediate deployment during a physical check?

options.A: A flashing red warning light on the console
options.B: A continuous auditory alarm sounding from the unit
options.C: A status indicator light showing a green checkmark or ready signal
options.D: A blank screen with no lights illuminated to save battery

explanation: A status indicator showing a green check or ready signal confirms that the AED has passed its internal self-tests and is ready for use. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h7)

question: What is a key nursing priority immediately after a patient achieves return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)?

options.A: Discharging the patient home immediately
options.B: Monitoring vital signs, managing airway/oxygenation, and preparing for transfer to the ICU
options.C: Removing all intravenous lines to prevent infection
options.D: Completing an incident report for the hospital director

explanation: Post-resuscitation care focuses on stabilizing the patient, managing airway and oxygenation, monitoring vitals, and arranging for intensive care monitoring. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h8)

question: Which of the following details must be included in the nurse's documentation of an AED resuscitation event?

options.A: The brand name and serial number of the hospital bed
options.B: The exact time the AED was applied, rhythm analyses, and shocks delivered
options.C: The financial cost of the electrode pads used
options.D: The names of all visitors present in the room during arrest

explanation: Accurate clinical documentation requires recording specific event timelines, AED deployment details like analyses and shocks, and the patient's response. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h8)

question: What is a primary advantage of infrared thermometers in clinical nursing practice?

options.A: They require prolonged contact with mucosal membranes
options.B: They provide rapid temperature assessments within seconds
options.C: They contain safe amounts of liquid mercury for calibration
options.D: They eliminate the need for any infection control protocols

explanation: Infrared thermometers capture thermal radiation to provide fast readings within seconds, which is crucial for busy clinical settings and rapid triage. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h1)

question: How do infrared thermometers assess body temperature compared to traditional glass thermometers?

options.A: By measuring thermal radiation emitted from targeted body surfaces
options.B: By conducting heat directly through mercury expansion in a glass tube
options.C: By chemical reaction with sweat on the patient's forehead
options.D: By electrical resistance changes inside the oral cavity

explanation: Unlike contact devices that use conduction, infrared thermometers detect the thermal radiation naturally emitted from the body surface. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h1)

question: What component inside an infrared thermometer absorbs focused thermal radiation and converts it into an electrical voltage?

options.A: A mercury bulb
options.B: A thermopile
options.C: A glass lens
options.D: An electrochemical cell

explanation: The thermopile is the specific sensor component that absorbs the focused infrared radiation and converts it into a measurable electrical signal. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h2)

question: What does an infrared thermometer actually measure before calculating core temperature?

options.A: Internal core blood pressure
options.B: Thermal radiation emitted from the body surface
options.C: The electrical resistance of sweat glands
options.D: Atmospheric barometric pressure

explanation: Infrared thermometers measure the thermal radiation emitted from the surface of the body and use algorithms to estimate core temperature. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h2)

question: Why is the tympanic membrane considered an ideal site for reflecting core body temperature?

options.A: It shares a blood supply with the hypothalamus
options.B: It is completely immune to environmental air drafts
options.C: It requires no anatomical manipulation of the ear
options.D: It is directly exposed to external ambient air

explanation: The tympanic membrane shares a vascular supply with the hypothalamus, making it an accurate reflection of the body's internal core temperature. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h3)

question: What anatomical landmark is targeted when using a temporal artery thermometer?

options.A: The external auditory meatus
options.B: The superficial temporal artery across the forehead
options.C: The carotid pulse point in the neck
options.D: The sublingual pocket under the tongue

explanation: Temporal artery thermometers scan across the forehead to detect thermal emissions from the superficial temporal artery. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h3)

question: When is the use of a tympanic infrared thermometer contraindicated?

options.A: When the patient is sleeping peacefully
options.B: When excessive cerumen or acute otitis media is present
options.C: When the patient has an elevated respiratory rate
options.D: When assessing an adult in an emergency ward

explanation: Excessive cerumen or middle ear infections like otitis media block or alter infrared emissions, making tympanic readings inaccurate. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h4)

question: Which condition would interfere with the accuracy of a temporal artery thermometer?

options.A: Severe perspiration or heavy skin moisture on the forehead
options.B: Mild elevation in systemic blood pressure
options.C: A normal clean outer ear canal
options.D: Patient age over 65 years old

explanation: Heavy perspiration cools the skin through evaporation, leading to falsely lowered temperature readings on a temporal scan. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h4)

question: How should the nurse position the pinna when taking a tympanic temperature on an adult patient?

options.A: Upward and backward
options.B: Downward and forward
options.C: Straight outward
options.D: Downward and backward

explanation: Pulling the adult pinna upward and backward straightens the curved ear canal, allowing the sensor a clear line of sight to the tympanic membrane. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h5)

question: What is the correct final movement when executing a temporal artery temperature measurement?

options.A: Pressing the probe firmly into the external ear canal
options.B: Sliding the device across the forehead and touching behind the earlobe
options.C: Holding the device stationary over the bridge of the nose
options.D: Swiping the thermometer rapidly across the patient's neck

explanation: The correct temporal scanning technique involves sliding the device across the forehead to the hairline and touching behind the earlobe while the button is depressed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h5)

question: How can lying on one side for a prolonged period affect a patient's infrared temperature reading?

options.A: It lowers the temperature due to increased air circulation
options.B: It artificially elevates the temperature on the exposed side due to trapped heat
options.C: It permanently damages the temporal artery bed
options.D: It has no effect on surface thermometry readings

explanation: Lying on one side traps body heat against the pillow, causing localized warming that can falsely elevate readings on that side of the head. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h6)

question: What should a nurse do if a patient has just entered the clinic from a very cold outdoor environment?

options.A: Take the temporal temperature immediately to catch baseline fever
options.B: Allow the patient time to acclimate to room temperature before measuring
options.C: Use a tympanic thermometer without a probe cover to speed up the process
options.D: Assume the patient is hypothermic and start active rewarming

explanation: Exposure to extreme external temperatures temporarily alters skin and ear canal temperatures, requiring an acclimate period for accurate readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h6)

question: What solution is commonly recommended for cleaning the lens and body of an infrared thermometer?

options.A: Strong chlorine bleach concentrate
options.B: 70% isopropyl alcohol on a lint-free wipe
options.C: Hot soapy water with complete submersion
options.D: Hydrogen peroxide solution soaked for two hours

explanation: 70% isopropyl alcohol on a lint-free wipe is standard for safely disinfecting the housing and lens without damaging internal optical components. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h7)

question: Why must nurses strictly adhere to using single-use disposable probe covers?

options.A: To prevent cross-contamination and healthcare-associated infections
options.B: To ensure the device battery remains fully charged
options.C: To prevent the infrared sensor from detecting room drafts
options.D: To calibrate the device automatically before each patient

explanation: Disposable probe covers act as a barrier to prevent the transmission of microbes between patients, maintaining infection control standards. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h7)

question: What essential details must be included when documenting an infrared temperature reading in a patient's chart?

options.A: Only the numerical value and the nurse's initials
options.B: The numerical value, route used, date, time, and relevant context
options.C: The brand name of the thermometer and battery serial number
options.D: The patient's insurance details and room temperature

explanation: Complete documentation requires the temperature value, measurement route, timestamp, and pertinent clinical context for accurate tracking. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h8)

question: How should a nurse interpret an infrared temperature reading in clinical practice?

options.A: As an absolute measurement that requires no further clinical context
options.B: As an estimated core temperature to be evaluated alongside patient presentation
options.C: As an exact direct measurement of pulmonary artery blood temperature
options.D: As an unreliable value that should always be ignored in adults

explanation: Infrared readings are estimates of core temperature and must always be interpreted in conjunction with the patient's overall clinical presentation and baseline. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h8)

question: What is the primary function of a mechanical ventilator?

options.A: To cure the underlying respiratory disease
options.B: To support or completely take over respiratory function
options.C: To permanently replace native lung tissue
options.D: To administer intravenous medications directly to the alveoli

explanation: A mechanical ventilator does not cure the underlying disease but rather provides critical support or takes over breathing to ensure gas exchange. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h1)

question: Which of the following is an example of invasive mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Continuous positive airway pressure via nasal mask
options.B: Bilevel positive airway pressure via face mask
options.C: Ventilation delivered via an endotracheal tube
options.D: Oxygen administration via nasal cannula

explanation: Invasive mechanical ventilation involves an artificial airway that enters the trachea, such as an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy tube. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h1)

question: Which condition is a classic example of hypoxemic (type 1) respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.B: Opioid drug overdose
options.C: Myasthenia gravis crisis
options.D: Chronic hypercapnic COPD

explanation: Hypoxemic respiratory failure is characterized by inadequate oxygenation, which is a hallmark of acute respiratory distress syndrome and severe pneumonia. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h2)

question: What is a key clinical sign indicating that a patient may soon require mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Calm demeanor and slow, even breathing
options.B: Use of accessory muscles and severe tachypnea
options.C: Elevated oxygen saturation of 99% on room air
options.D: Normal arterial blood gas pH values

explanation: Accessory muscle use and severe tachypnea indicate respiratory fatigue and impending failure, often prompting the need for mechanical ventilation. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h2)

question: In which ventilator mode does the machine deliver a set breath in response to the patient's inspiratory effort, but deliver a timed mandatory breath if the patient does not initiate one?

options.A: Assist-Control (AC) mode
options.B: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)
options.C: Pure Controlled Mechanical Ventilation (CMV)
options.D: Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) alone

explanation: Assist-Control mode allows the patient to trigger breaths, but guarantees a minimum respiratory rate by delivering machine breaths if the patient fails to initiate them. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP)?

options.A: To completely paralyze the respiratory muscles
options.B: To keep alveoli open at the end of expiration and improve oxygenation
options.C: To flush carbon dioxide out of the ventilator tubing
options.D: To rapidly lower the patient's blood pressure

explanation: PEEP applies positive pressure at the end of exhalation to prevent alveolar collapse, thereby improving lung compliance and oxygenation. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h3)

question: What is the most immediate clinical check a nurse should perform after an endotracheal tube is secured and connected to a ventilator?

options.A: Measure the patient's daily caloric intake
options.B: Auscultate bilateral breath sounds and check chest symmetry
options.C: Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram
options.D: Check the patient's deep tendon reflexes

explanation: Auscultating bilateral breath sounds and observing chest symmetry ensures the endotracheal tube is correctly placed in the trachea and not inadvertently in the right mainstem bronchus or esophagus. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h4)

question: Why is continuous hemodynamic monitoring important when a patient is placed on mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Positive pressure ventilation can decrease venous return and impact cardiac output
options.B: Ventilators automatically induce severe hypertension
options.C: Mechanical ventilation has no effect on the cardiovascular system
options.D: It prevents the patient from moving their arms

explanation: Positive pressure inside the chest increases intrathoracic pressure, which can reduce venous return to the heart and cause hypotension or decreased cardiac output. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h4)

question: How often should routine oral care using chlorhexidine be performed for a mechanically ventilated patient to help prevent complications?

options.A: Once a week
options.B: Only when family members request it
options.C: Regularly as part of standard bundled ventilator care
options.D: Never, as it increases the risk of extubation

explanation: Regular oral care with chlorhexidine is a core element of ventilator care bundles designed to reduce bacterial colonization and prevent infections like VAP. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h5)

question: Why is eye care essential for a heavily sedated, mechanically ventilated patient?

options.A: To improve visual acuity after extubation
options.B: To prevent corneal ulceration due to absent blinking reflexes
options.C: To lower intraocular pressure caused by ventilator pressures
options.D: To check for neurological pupil reactivity every hour

explanation: Sedated patients often lose their normal blink reflex and incomplete eyelid closure can lead to corneal drying and ulceration, making eye care essential. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h5)

question: What is the recommended angle for elevating the head of the bed for a mechanically ventilated patient to help prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia?

options.A: Flat at 0 degrees
options.B: 10 to 15 degrees
options.C: 30 to 45 degrees
options.D: 90 degrees fully upright

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees helps prevent the aspiration of oral and gastric secretions into the lower respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is the target range for endotracheal tube cuff pressure to prevent both tracheal tissue damage and micro-aspiration?

options.A: 5 to 10 cmH2O
options.B: 20 to 30 cmH2O
options.C: 40 to 50 cmH2O
options.D: 60 to 70 cmH2O

explanation: Maintaining cuff pressure between 20 and 30 cmH2O seals the airway effectively against aspiration while avoiding excessive pressure that can cause tracheal necrosis. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is a primary clinical indicator that a patient is ready to begin the weaning process from mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Requirement of high-dose vasopressor medications
options.B: Improvement in the underlying condition and stable hemodynamics
options.C: Complete absence of any cough reflex
options.D: Continuous deep sedation with high-dose paralytics

explanation: Patients are candidates for weaning when their primary illness has improved, hemodynamics are stable, and they meet specific respiratory and neurological criteria. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h7)

question: Which finding during a Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT) indicates that the patient is failing the test and weaning should be stopped?

options.A: Stable heart rate and blood pressure
options.B: Relaxed facial expression and normal respiratory rate
options.C: Severe tachypnea, diaphoresis, and oxygen desaturation
options.D: Ability to follow commands and communicate

explanation: Signs of respiratory fatigue such as tachypnea, diaphoresis, and desaturation indicate the patient cannot tolerate independent breathing and the SBT should be halted. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of continuous cardiac monitoring in clinical practice?

options.A: To replace the need for manual blood pressure measurement
options.B: To continuously observe cardiac electrical activity and detect arrhythmias
options.C: To deliver electrical cardioversion automatically
options.D: To diagnose electrolyte imbalances without laboratory testing

explanation: Cardiac monitoring is used to continuously observe the heart's electrical activity to detect arrhythmias and guide clinical interventions. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is cardiac monitoring considered a critical skill for nursing professionals?

options.A: It allows nurses to identify subtle rhythm changes before they progress to cardiac arrest
options.B: It eliminates the requirement for physical patient assessments
options.C: It is only required for patients with diagnosed neurological disorders
options.D: It prevents all forms of hospital-acquired infections

explanation: Continuous observation helps nurses catch subtle changes in heart rate and rhythm early, preventing sudden clinical deterioration. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which waveform on the ECG represents atrial depolarization?

options.A: T wave
options.B: QRS complex
options.C: P wave
options.D: ST segment

explanation: The P wave corresponds to atrial depolarization, marking the spread of electrical impulses through the atria. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h2)

question: What does the QRS complex signify on a standard electrocardiogram?

options.A: Atrial repolarization
options.B: Ventricular depolarization
options.C: Atrial contraction recovery
options.D: Ventricular filling time

explanation: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization, which triggers ventricular contraction. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h2)

question: Where should the white electrode be placed in a standard 5-lead cardiac monitoring configuration?

options.A: Left arm
options.B: Right arm
options.C: Left leg
options.D: Chest wall

explanation: Using standard mnemonics, the white electrode is placed on the right arm (RA). [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of telemetry monitoring over traditional bedside monitors?

options.A: It measures blood pressure automatically without cuffs
options.B: It allows ambulatory patients to be continuously monitored while moving
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for electrode skin preparation
options.D: It provides 12-lead diagnostic capability for acute myocardial infarction

explanation: Telemetry monitoring uses wireless transmitters, enabling stable patients to ambulate while nursing staff continuously observe their rhythm from a central station. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why is skin preparation before electrode application important?

options.A: It increases skin pigmentation for better visibility
options.B: It reduces electrical resistance and ensures secure adhesion
options.C: It permanently cures skin allergies to electrode gel
options.D: It replaces the need for baseline vital signs

explanation: Cleaning and drying the skin removes oils and moisture, reducing electrical resistance and helping electrodes adhere properly for clear signal transmission. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is an important nursing action to prevent skin breakdown during prolonged cardiac monitoring?

options.A: Applying adhesive remover directly into open wounds
options.B: Leaving the same electrodes on without inspection for weeks
options.C: Rotating electrode sites and inspecting the skin regularly
options.D: Never removing electrodes once applied

explanation: Rotating electrode sites and inspecting the skin daily helps prevent irritation, breakdown, and allergic reactions from adhesives. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the normal heart rate range for a Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR)?

options.A: 40 to 60 beats per minute
options.B: 60 to 100 beats per minute
options.C: 100 to 140 beats per minute
options.D: Less than 50 beats per minute

explanation: A normal sinus rhythm originates in the SA node with a regular rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which of the following is a hallmark feature of atrial fibrillation on an ECG strip?

options.A: Regularly spaced narrow QRS complexes with distinct P waves
options.B: An irregularly irregular rhythm with absent distinct P waves
options.C: A heart rate consistently below 50 beats per minute
options.D: Prolonged PR intervals exceeding 0.30 seconds

explanation: Atrial fibrillation is characterized by an irregularly irregular ventricular response and chaotic atrial activity where distinct P waves are absent. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary action a nurse should take when an alarm sounds indicating a lethal arrhythmia on the cardiac monitor?

options.A: Immediately silence the alarm and turn off the machine
options.B: Assess the patient first for pulse, breathing, and responsiveness
options.C: Document that the patient has suffered a cardiac arrest without looking at them
options.D: Wait for 30 minutes to see if the rhythm corrects itself

explanation: The golden rule of cardiac monitoring is to always assess the patient first to rule out artifact and confirm true clinical emergency before taking action. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is a frequent cause of monitor artifact resembling abnormal electrical activity?

options.A: Properly applied and fresh electrode pads
options.B: Patient movement, muscle tremors, or loose electrode connections
options.C: Stable patient hemodynamic status
options.D: Correctly configured alarm parameters

explanation: Patient motion, muscle tremors, shivering, and loose leads frequently introduce electrical artifact onto the monitor screen. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is 'alarm fatigue' in the context of nursing care with cardiac monitors?

options.A: A condition where monitors run out of battery power
options.B: Desensitization of staff due to frequent alarms, leading to delayed responses or ignored alerts
options.C: Physical exhaustion experienced by patients wearing ECG leads
options.D: The technical failure of monitor speakers during night shifts

explanation: Alarm fatigue occurs when frequent, often non-critical alarms desensitize staff, increasing the risk of ignoring or missing critical alerts. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following is a key nursing responsibility regarding cardiac monitor documentation?

options.A: Never recording rhythm strips in the patient's chart
options.B: Systematically recording baseline strips per shift and documenting significant rhythm changes with patient status
options.C: Only documenting alarms that sound during the night
options.D: Delegating all rhythm interpretation and documentation to housekeeping staff

explanation: Nurses are responsible for systematically documenting baseline rhythms, recording changes, and noting the corresponding clinical status of the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary advantage of an infusion pump over a gravity-fed intravenous line?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for nursing documentation.
options.B: It delivers fluids at a precisely regulated rate regardless of patient movement or bag height.
options.C: It removes the need to monitor the intravenous insertion site.
options.D: It prevents all forms of infiltration and phlebitis automatically.

explanation: Infusion pumps utilize a mechanized system to maintain a precise flow rate, overcoming variables like patient movement and bag height that affect gravity drips. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which category of medications makes the use of infusion pumps particularly critical in clinical practice?

options.A: Oral vitamins and mineral supplements
options.B: Topical barrier creams and ointments
options.C: High-alert medications such as vasopressors and insulin
options.D: Routine maintenance oral analgesics

explanation: High-alert medications require precise delivery because small fluctuations in the flow rate can lead to severe clinical complications like extreme blood pressure changes or hypoglycemia. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which type of infusion pump is best suited for delivering very small volumes of potent medication at low, continuous rates, such as in neonatal care?

options.A: Volumetric infusion pump
options.B: Syringe pump
options.C: Elastomeric pump
options.D: Gravity roller clamp

explanation: Syringe pumps hold a syringe instead of a bag and are designed to deliver small volumes at precise, low rates, making them ideal for neonates and critical care titrations. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the specific safety feature of a Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) pump that prevents a patient from overdosing?

options.A: A built-in blood pressure monitor that stops the drug
options.B: A lock-out interval that restricts continuous bolus delivery
options.C: An audible alarm that sounds whenever the patient touches the button
options.D: A maximum volume limit of 5 milliliters per day

explanation: PCA pumps use a programmed lock-out interval to prevent the patient from administering another dose too soon, thereby avoiding accidental drug overdose. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary function of a downstream sensor in an infusion pump?

options.A: To detect blockages located between the pump and the patient's vascular access site
options.B: To measure the room temperature around the patient's bed
options.C: To detect fluid shortages in the hanging IV bag
options.D: To monitor the patient's heart rate and oxygen saturation

explanation: Downstream sensors are specifically positioned to detect occlusions and blockages between the pump mechanism and the patient's IV insertion site. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h3)

question: How do standard peristaltic infusion pumps propel fluid through the intravenous tubing?

options.A: By applying continuous heat to expand the fluid molecules
options.B: By using mechanical fingers that sequentially compress and relax the tubing
options.C: By spinning the IV bag at high centrifugal speeds
options.D: By relying solely on gravity to pull fluid past a magnetic valve

explanation: Peristaltic pumps use mechanical fingers that compress and relax the specialized tubing in a wave-like motion to push fluid forward in precise amounts. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the standard unit of measurement typically programmed into a volumetric infusion pump for general fluid delivery?

options.A: Milliliters per hour (mL/hr)
options.B: Drops per minute (gtt/min)
options.C: Liters per twenty-four hours (L/24hr)
options.D: Milligrams per minute (mg/min)

explanation: Volumetric infusion pumps are digitally programmed to deliver fluids in exact milliliters per hour (mL/hr). [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why is an independent double-check by a second nurse especially important when programming high-alert medications?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any documentation in the patient chart.
options.B: It prevents calculation and programming errors that could result in patient harm.
options.C: it allows the primary nurse to leave the unit for a break.
options.D: It automatically adjusts the pump pressure based on vein size.

explanation: An independent double-check involving two nurses helps catch mathematical, decimal, or programming errors before high-alert medications are administered to the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary action a nurse should take when an infusion pump alarm sounds?

options.A: Unplug the pump from the wall outlet immediately
options.B: Press the silence button and ignore it if the fluid is still dripping
options.C: Investigate the cause of the alarm immediately and resolve the issue
options.D: Turn off the pump and remove the intravenous catheter

explanation: Alarms indicate a disruption in the infusion system and must never be ignored; the nurse must investigate and resolve the underlying cause promptly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h5)

question: How often should the nurse inspect the intravenous insertion site for signs of infiltration or phlebitis during pump-regulated therapy?

options.A: Only when the patient is discharged from the hospital
options.B: Regularly per hospital policy and during routine assessments
options.C: Once a week during routine dressing changes
options.D: Only when the infusion bag is completely empty

explanation: Routine site assessments per hospital policy are necessary to catch early signs of complications like infiltration, extravasation, or phlebitis. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h5)

question: What does an occlusion alarm on an infusion pump typically indicate?

options.A: The infusion bag is completely empty.
options.B: There is a blockage or restriction somewhere in the fluid pathway.
options.C: The battery is fully charged and functioning normally.
options.D: The medication has finished infusing completely.

explanation: An occlusion alarm signals a blockage in the system, which can be caused by kinked tubing, closed clamps, or a positional IV catheter. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h6)

question: How should a nurse respond when an air-in-line alarm is triggered?

options.A: Disconnect the patient and discard the entire intravenous setup.
options.B: Increase the flow rate to push the air through the vein quickly.
options.C: Inspect the tubing, clear any bubbles according to safety protocols, and ensure no air enters the patient.
options.D: Ignore the alarm because small amounts of air are harmless.

explanation: The nurse must inspect the line to locate and manage air bubbles safely, preventing them from reaching the patient's vascular system and causing an air embolism. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h6)

question: How long should a nurse scrub a needleless connector with an antiseptic wipe before accessing an infusion line?

options.A: 2 seconds
options.B: 5 seconds
options.C: 15 seconds
options.D: 60 seconds

explanation: Standard infection control protocols recommend scrubbing needleless connectors with an antiseptic wipe for at least 15 seconds and allowing them to dry to ensure proper microbial decontamination. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h7)

question: Why must infusion tubing used for total parenteral nutrition (TPN) or lipid emulsions be changed more frequently than standard crystalloid IV tubing?

options.A: Lipids and TPN rapidly support bacterial and fungal growth.
options.B: Lipid solutions dissolve the plastic material of the infusion tubing.
options.C: TPN fluids stain the clear tubing and obscure air bubble detection.
options.D: Manufacturers require daily replacement for warranty purposes.

explanation: Nutrient-rich solutions like TPN and lipids provide an ideal medium for rapid microbial proliferation, necessitating more frequent tubing changes to prevent infection. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a syringe driver in clinical practice?

options.A: To deliver rapid intermittent intravenous boluses
options.B: To ensure continuous, controlled delivery of precise medication volumes
options.C: To measure blood pressure continuously alongside medication infusion
options.D: To replace the need for regular nursing vital sign assessments

explanation: A syringe driver is specifically designed for the continuous and controlled administration of medications in precise volumes over time. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h1)

question: In which clinical areas are syringe drivers most frequently utilized for continuous symptom management?

options.A: Orthopedic outpatient clinics
options.B: Palliative care and oncology
options.C: General routine physical check-ups
options.D: Ophthalmology surgical suites

explanation: Syringe drivers are invaluable in palliative care and oncology for steady symptom management like continuous pain control. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary clinical indication for initiating a syringe driver?

options.A: Patient preference for daily oral vitamin supplements
options.B: Compromised oral route due to severe dysphagia or persistent vomiting
options.C: Requirement for rapid high-volume fluid resuscitation
options.D: Uncomplicated hypertension managed with daily tablets

explanation: A syringe driver is indicated when the oral route is compromised, such as during severe dysphagia or persistent vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h2)

question: Why is the subcutaneous route via a syringe driver preferred over repeated intramuscular injections?

options.A: It requires no monitoring or site inspections
options.B: It spares the patient the distress of repeated painful injections and provides stable absorption
options.C: It allows for unlimited high-volume fluid administration instantly
options.D: It eliminates the need for any compatibility checks

explanation: Using a syringe driver avoids repeated painful intramuscular injections and provides consistent, steady drug absorption. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h2)

question: Why is it important to use only the specific brand and size of syringe recommended by the device manufacturer?

options.A: Different syringes have varying barrel dimensions that affect infusion rate accuracy
options.B: Manufacturer-approved syringes are always free of any cost
options.C: Plastic syringes from other brands will melt inside the machine
options.D: Non-approved syringes prevent the machine from ever turning on

explanation: Variations in syringe barrel dimensions across brands can alter delivery accuracy and lead to incorrect dosing. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h3)

question: What is the function of the keypad lockout feature on a syringe driver?

options.A: To increase the battery life during transport
options.B: To prevent accidental or unauthorized alteration of programmed infusion rates
options.C: To automatically lock the syringe barrel into the cradle
options.D: To silence occlusion alarms permanently

explanation: The keypad lockout feature prevents accidental or unauthorized changes to the infusion settings by patients or visitors. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h3)

question: What critical action must be taken when mixing multiple medications in a single syringe for a driver?

options.A: Ensure complete drug compatibility to prevent precipitation
options.B: Heat the syringe in hot water to dissolve all powders
options.C: Prime the extension line with air to create a buffer
options.D: Ignore manufacturer syringe size guidelines

explanation: Checking drug compatibility is vital because mixing incompatible drugs can cause precipitation, blocking the line or altering potency. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h4)

question: Why is priming the extension line carefully an essential safety check?

options.A: To test if the plastic is waterproof
options.B: To expel air bubbles and ensure immediate delivery upon starting
options.C: To empty the entire contents of the syringe before attachment
options.D: To lubricate the mechanical drive motor

explanation: Priming removes air bubbles and ensures that the medication reaches the patient without delay when the infusion starts. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h4)

question: What safety practice is strongly recommended when programming and setting up a syringe driver?

options.A: Single-nurse verification to save time
options.B: Dual-nurse check of programmed parameters against the prescription
options.C: Leaving the infusion rate unverified until the next shift
options.D: Programming the device while disconnected from power sources only

explanation: A dual-nurse check helps catch programming errors and ensures patient safety before starting the infusion. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h5)

question: How does the nurse confirm that the syringe driver has successfully started delivering medication?

options.A: By listening for a continuous loud alarm tone
options.B: By observing the running indicator or moving graphic showing the mechanism is active
options.C: By immediately flushing the line with 20ml of sterile water
options.D: By feeling the patient's skin for warmth at the device site

explanation: Observing the running indicator light or moving graphic confirms that the driver is actively advancing the plunger. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h5)

question: What signs at the infusion site should prompt immediate nursing intervention and possible site replacement?

options.A: Normal skin color and lack of pain
options.B: Swelling, redness, pain, or fluid leakage
options.C: Coolness of the surrounding unaffected skin
options.D: Clear visibility of the subcutaneous needle

explanation: Swelling, redness, pain, or leakage indicate site complications like infiltration or displacement, requiring site replacement. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h6)

question: How often should subcutaneous infusion sites typically be inspected and managed in clinical practice?

options.A: Once every two weeks
options.B: Only when the patient complains of severe pain
options.C: At least every shift or per hospital protocol
options.D: Immediately after discharge only

explanation: Infusion sites must be inspected at least every shift to catch early signs of complications or site failure. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the first step a nurse should take when an occlusion alarm sounds on a syringe driver?

options.A: Turn off the device permanently and switch to oral meds
options.B: Check the patient's site, extension line for kinks, and closed clamps
options.C: Increase the infusion pressure setting to bypass the blockage
options.D: Disconnect the line and flush with a high-pressure syringe

explanation: The nurse must systematically check for kinks, closed clamps, or site issues before taking further corrective actions. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h7)

question: What does a near-finish alarm signify during the operation of a syringe driver?

options.A: The battery is completely depleted and the machine is shutting down
options.B: The syringe is nearly empty, allowing time to prepare a replacement
options.C: An occlusion has occurred in the extension tubing
options.D: The infusion has been running at twice the prescribed rate

explanation: A near-finish alarm warns that the syringe is almost empty, enabling nurses to prepare the next syringe proactively. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following details must be documented when managing a syringe driver infusion?

options.A: Only the brand name of the syringe driver machine
options.B: Medication name, dosage, diluent, infusion rate, and site inspection results
options.C: The patient's favorite meal preferences
options.D: The cost of the disposable extension lines

explanation: Comprehensive documentation must include drug details, dosage, diluent, rate, and site condition for accountability and safety. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h8)

question: What infection control practice should always be applied when changing a syringe or handling infusion lines?

options.A: Hand hygiene and aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT)
options.B: Soaking all equipment in hot tap water
options.C: Wearing sterile surgical gowns for all routine checks
options.D: Avoiding gloves to maintain better finger dexterity

explanation: Strict hand hygiene and aseptic techniques prevent microbial contamination and subsequent site infections. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary clinical advantage of using a bedside glucometer over standard laboratory blood glucose testing?

options.A: Requiring no calibration or quality control checks
options.B: Providing rapid results to guide immediate care
options.C: Providing absolute definitive diagnostic accuracy
options.D: Eliminating the need for strict infection control

explanation: Bedside glucometers deliver immediate blood glucose values, allowing healthcare providers to quickly identify and treat critical imbalances like severe hypoglycemia. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is blood glucose monitoring frequently ordered for a patient presenting to the emergency department with an acute altered mental status?

options.A: To screen for infectious organisms causing meningitis
options.B: To confirm a definitive diagnosis of chronic kidney disease
options.C: To evaluate the patient for underlying severe hypoglycemia
options.D: To determine the exact baseline hemoglobin A1c level

explanation: Neuroglycopenia caused by low blood glucose can rapidly mimic other neurological emergencies, making immediate blood glucose screening mandatory in altered mental states. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which chemical substance located on the test strip reacts directly with the glucose in a blood sample?

options.A: Buffered liquid hydrochloric acid
options.B: Sterile isotonic sodium chloride
options.C: Specific enzymes like glucose oxidase
options.D: Anticoagulant potassium oxalate

explanation: Test strips contain specialized enzymes that catalyze a reaction with glucose, generating the electrical or optical signal the meter reads. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h2)

question: How does the internal mechanism of a standard electronic glucometer translate the blood sample into a digital reading?

options.A: It measures the exact temperature shift of the surrounding skin
options.B: It measures the electrical current generated by the enzymatic reaction
options.C: It calculates the specific centrifugation speed of red blood cells
options.D: It weighs the total volume of blood applied to the reactive pad

explanation: Most modern meters utilize amperometric biosensors that quantify the electrical current produced when glucose reacts with the strip enzymes. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h2)

question: What is the correct action regarding skin preparation before performing a capillary blood glucose puncture?

options.A: Ensure the cleaned skin is completely dry before puncturing
options.B: Leave a generous pool of wet alcohol on the finger for lubrication
options.C: Apply heavy emollient lotion to soften the hardened skin pad
options.D: Scrub the puncture site vigorously with a povidone-iodine pad

explanation: Residual alcohol can dilute the blood sample or cause hemolysis, resulting in inaccurate readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h3)

question: Why is having a patient wash their hands with warm water preferred over an alcohol swab alone prior to capillary sampling?

options.A: It completely sterilizes the epidermis to prevent systemic bacteremia
options.B: It eliminates the necessity of wearing clean disposable gloves
options.C: It neutralizes any acidic pH present within the dermal layers
options.D: It removes external sugar residues and improves local blood circulation

explanation: Handwashing removes microscopic food particles or drink residue that could falsely elevate the reading, while warmth increases local blood flow for an easier sample. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h3)

question: While obtaining a capillary blood sample from a patient's finger, you notice the blood droplet is difficult to express. What is the safest technique to encourage blood flow?

options.A: Gently massage proximally from the base of the finger toward the tip
options.B: Apply strong suction using a sterile syringe barrel to the puncture
options.C: Milks and squeeze the fingertip aggressively to force out fluid
options.D: Prick the exact center of the fingertip pad a second time

explanation: Gentle proximal massage encourages blood flow without expressing excess tissue fluid, which dilutes the sample and skews the glucose reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which anatomical area of the finger is the preferred site for capillary blood sampling to minimize patient discomfort?

options.A: The thick skin directly over the nail bed
options.B: The soft flexion crease of the distal joint
options.C: The lateral or side parts of the fingertip
options.D: The direct center of the fleshy finger pad

explanation: The sides of the fingers have fewer nerve endings than the central pads, making the puncture less painful for the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which blood glucose value typically serves as the threshold for defining hypoglycemia requiring immediate clinical action?

options.A: Above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
options.B: Between 6.0 and 7.8 mmol/L
options.C: Below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL)
options.D: Between 8.0 and 10.0 mmol/L

explanation: Glycemic values dropping below 3.9 mmol/L are clinically classified as hypoglycemia, necessitating prompt carbohydrate administration or other medical correction. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why must a nurse correlate a glucometer reading with the patient's physical presentation rather than relying solely on the number?

options.A: Clinical symptoms reflect the physiological impact and safety of the patient
options.B: Laboratory equipment is legally required to confirm every normal value
options.C: Digital meters display reversed numbers when batteries are low
options.D: Glucometers never register correct values during morning shifts

explanation: Patients adapt differently to fluctuating glucose levels; a person with chronic high blood sugar may experience symptoms at higher thresholds, while asymptomatic readings still demand contextual evaluation. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a quality control check using control solutions on a glucometer?

options.A: To clean dried organic blood protein from the optical sensors
options.B: To verify that the meter and test strips are working accurately
options.C: To recalibrate the internal battery voltage of the digital display
options.D: To clear the internal memory storage of past patient readings

explanation: Control solutions contain known glucose levels that test whether the meter and strips produce expected, accurate results. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h6)

question: Under which circumstance is a quality control test most critically required?

options.A: When opening a fresh vial of unused test strips
options.B: Every time a different nurse touches the handheld device
options.C: Before washing hands at the start of a clinical shift
options.D: Immediately after checking a patient with normal glucose

explanation: New batches or vials of strips can react differently due to manufacturing variations, making quality control testing essential upon opening. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the most common consequence of applying an insufficient drop of blood to a capillary test strip?

options.A: Immediate destruction of the internal battery housing
options.B: A permanently locked meter requiring factory reset
options.C: A falsely elevated reading due to atmospheric oxidation
options.D: An error message or a falsely low glucose reading

explanation: If the reaction area on the strip is not completely covered by blood, the meter cannot measure the reaction properly, often displaying an error or an inaccurate low value. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h7)

question: Which of the following environmental conditions can severely compromise the integrity of glucometer test strips?

options.A: Storage in a dark, cool, dry medication drawer
options.B: Keeping the container lid tightly sealed after use
options.C: Maintaining room temperature within specified limits
options.D: Exposure to excessive humidity and high heat

explanation: Humidity and heat degrade the sensitive chemical reagents on test strips, leading to unreliable and inaccurate glucose results. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the correct practice regarding the handling of used lancets after obtaining a capillary blood sample?

options.A: Recap the needle securely and place it in the general trash
options.B: Dispose of them immediately into a rigid sharps container
options.C: Clean the lancet tip with alcohol and store it for reuse
options.D: Leave the lancet on the bedside tray for the next test

explanation: To prevent accidental needlestick injuries and bloodborne pathogen transmission, used sharps must be discarded immediately into a designated container without recapping. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h8)

question: Why is it mandatory to clean and disinfect the exterior of a shared ward glucometer between different patients?

options.A: To calibrate the internal electronic sensors automatically
options.B: To prevent the battery compartment from accumulating dust
options.C: To prevent the transmission of bloodborne pathogens and cross-infection
options.D: To ensure the digital screen displays clear numerical values

explanation: Glucometers are frequently handled and exposed to blood droplets; disinfecting them between patients stops the spread of infectious agents in clinical units. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h8)

question: What does the abbreviation SpO2 represent in clinical practice?

options.A: Systemic pulse output two
options.B: Arterial oxygen saturation
options.C: Specific pressure of oxygen
options.D: Serum protein oxidation

explanation: SpO2 stands for arterial oxygen saturation, which is measured non-invasively by a pulse oximeter. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h1)

question: Why is relying solely on clinical cyanosis considered inadequate compared to pulse oximetry?

options.A: Cyanosis only appears after oxygen saturation has dropped to dangerously low levels.
options.B: Cyanosis requires laboratory blood draws to be confirmed.
options.C: Cyanosis only occurs in patients with pre-existing cardiac conditions.
options.D: Cyanosis is too expensive to monitor regularly.

explanation: Cyanosis is a late and unreliable indicator of hypoxia because it usually only becomes visible when oxygen saturation is already critically low. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which wavelength of light is primarily absorbed by oxygenated hemoglobin?

options.A: Infrared light at approximately 940 nm
options.B: Red light at approximately 660 nm
options.C: Ultraviolet light at 400 nm
options.D: Green light at 550 nm

explanation: Oxyhemoglobin absorbs more infrared light (around 940 nm), whereas deoxygenated hemoglobin absorbs more red light (around 660 nm). [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is the role of photoplethysmography in pulse oximetry?

options.A: To measure the exact core body temperature simultaneously
options.B: To differentiate light absorption by pulsatile arterial blood from non-pulsatile tissues
options.C: To deliver electrical impulses that stimulate peripheral circulation
options.D: To destroy abnormal hemoglobin molecules in the capillary bed

explanation: Photoplethysmography allows the device to isolate the fluctuating light absorption of pulsing arterial blood from surrounding static tissues like bone, skin, and veins. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h2)

question: What are the two primary light sources housed within a standard pulse oximeter probe?

options.A: Ultraviolet and microwave diodes
options.B: Red and infrared light-emitting diodes
options.C: Laser and fluorescent bulbs
options.D: X-ray and gamma emitters

explanation: Pulse oximeter probes use red and infrared light-emitting diodes (LEDs) to shine specific light wavelengths through the tissue. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the function of the photodetector in the pulse oximeter sensor?

options.A: It emits the light waves through the patient's finger.
options.B: It measures the intensity of light that passes through the tissue to the other side.
options.C: It warms up the capillary bed to improve local blood flow.
options.D: It calculates the patient's blood pressure automatically.

explanation: The photodetector acts as the receiver, measuring how much light successfully passes through the tissue after partial absorption by blood and structures. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following is a common clinical indication for pulse oximetry in Nigerian pediatric wards?

options.A: Uncomplicated simple bone fracture
options.B: Severe malaria or acute bronchiolitis
options.C: Routine dental check-ups
options.D: Chronic asymptomatic hypertension

explanation: Severe malaria, pneumonia, and bronchiolitis frequently cause respiratory compromise in children, making pulse oximetry essential for monitoring their oxygen status. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h4)

question: How does pulse oximetry assist nurses working in resource-constrained Nigerian healthcare facilities?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for physical respiratory assessments.
options.B: It helps prioritize critical patients and rationalize limited oxygen therapy administration.
options.C: It diagnoses the specific bacterial strain causing pneumonia.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any documentation or charting.

explanation: By providing objective oxygen saturation data, nurses can prioritize critically ill patients and ensure limited oxygen resources are used efficiently. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h4)

question: What physical feature on a patient's fingernail must be addressed before applying a standard finger probe?

options.A: Short nail length
options.B: Dark nail polish or artificial nails
options.C: Natural nail ridges
options.D: Moisture from sweat

explanation: Dark nail polish or artificial nails can block or absorb the light wavelengths, leading to inaccurate SpO2 readings and therefore must be removed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h5)

question: How can a nurse confirm that the pulse oximeter is receiving a reliable, high-quality signal?

options.A: By checking that the displayed pulse rate matches the patient's palpated pulse and observing a consistent waveform
options.B: By shaking the patient's hand vigorously
options.C: By turning off all lights in the hospital room
options.D: By wrapping adhesive tape tightly around the probe

explanation: A matching pulse rate and a steady, consistent plethysmographic waveform confirm that the oximeter is detecting a strong, reliable arterial pulse. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h5)

question: What SpO2 percentage range is generally considered normal for a healthy adult breathing room air?
explanation: Normal arterial oxygen saturation for healthy individuals typically falls between 95% and 100% on room air. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h6)

question: What immediate action is indicated when a patient's SpO2 reading drops below 90% on room air?

options.A: Discharge the patient home immediately
options.B: Document the finding and recheck the patient in 24 hours
options.C: Assess the patient, notify the physician, and prepare to administer supplemental oxygen
options.D: Remove the pulse oximeter and avoid further monitoring

question: How does carboxyhemoglobin, resulting from carbon monoxide poisoning, affect pulse oximetry readings?

options.C: It causes the device to switch to measuring blood pressure.
options.D: It has no effect on optical sensors.

explanation: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light similarly to oxyhemoglobin, causing the device to give a falsely high SpO2 reading despite true tissue hypoxia. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following physiological conditions is most likely to cause poor peripheral perfusion and weaken the oximeter signal?

options.A: Severe hypothermia or hypovolemic shock
options.B: High physical fitness and athletic conditioning
options.C: Normal hydration and relaxed resting state
options.D: Mild elevation in body temperature

explanation: Conditions like severe hypothermia and shock cause peripheral vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow to fingers and toes and weakening the pulse signal. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T6#GNS212_U4_T6_h7)

question: How often should adhesive pulse oximeter sensor sites typically be rotated to prevent skin breakdown?

options.B: Every 2 to 4 hours

options.D: Only when the patient complains of pain

question: Which of the following best describes the nurse's responsibility in patient education regarding pulse oximetry?

question: What is a primary benefit of automated patient beds regarding nursing personnel?

options.D: They allow nurses to work entirely remotely from home.

question: How do smart beds differ fundamentally from traditional hospital beds?

question: What is the clinical purpose of integrated load cells in smart beds?

question: Which component is responsible for powering the articulation and height adjustments of a smart bed?

options.D: Hydraulic fluid reservoirs

question: What is the primary purpose of healthcare simulation in nursing education?

question: Which of the following is classified as a low-fidelity simulator or task trainer?

question: What is a major advantage of simulation-based competency assessments before clinical placement?

options.D: Isometric ROM

question: What physiological benefit is achieved by facilitating synovial fluid circulation during ROM exercises?

options.A: Preservation of cartilage health
options.B: Direct increase in bone mineral density
options.C: Elimination of red blood cell destruction
options.D: Prevention of respiratory infections

explanation: Facilitating synovial fluid circulation through ROM exercises preserves cartilage health. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which type of exercise involves muscle contraction without changing the length of the muscle or moving the joint?

options.A: Isotonic exercise
options.B: Isometric exercise
options.C: Aerobic exercise
options.D: Isokinetic exercise

explanation: Isometric exercises involve muscle contraction without joint movement, making them useful for immobilized limbs. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of progressive resistance training?

options.A: Decreasing resting heart rate permanently
options.B: Stimulating cellular hypertrophy and neural adaptation
options.C: Causing permanent joint stiffness
options.D: Eliminating the need for dietary protein

explanation: Progressive resistance training challenges muscles with increasing loads, stimulating cellular hypertrophy and neural adaptation. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary role of dietary protein in muscle recovery?

options.A: Providing immediate water balance
options.B: Supplying amino acids for tissue remodeling and repair
options.C: Acting as the primary source of short-term cellular energy
options.D: Preventing all forms of bone fractures

explanation: Muscle tissue is remodeled and repaired using amino acids derived from dietary proteins. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h6)

question: What happens if a patient lacks sufficient caloric intake from carbohydrates and fats during recovery?

options.A: The body will use protein for energy instead of repair
options.B: Muscle mass will automatically increase
options.C: Hydration levels will stabilize instantly
options.D: The catabolic state will completely cease

explanation: Without sufficient carbohydrates and fats, the body burns protein for energy rather than using it for muscle repair. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h6)

question: How often should a bedridden patient typically be repositioned to prevent pressure ulcers and soft tissue damage?

options.A: Every 30 minutes
options.B: Every 2 hours
options.C: Every 6 hours
options.D: Once a day

explanation: Turning and repositioning the patient every two hours relieves sustained pressure on bony prominences. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h7)

question: Which nursing intervention helps prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT) caused by blood stasis in immobilized patients?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake completely
options.B: Using anti-embolism stockings and early ambulation
options.C: Applying hot packs continuously to the abdomen
options.D: Keeping the patient in a flat supine position

explanation: Anti-embolism stockings, compression devices, and early ambulation help prevent blood stasis and DVT. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the ultimate goal of musculoskeletal nursing education upon discharge?

options.A: Ensuring the patient remains entirely dependent on hospital staff
options.B: Fostering long-term functional independence and safe home care
options.C: Eliminating the need for any future physical activity
options.D: Reducing the patient's daily caloric requirements

explanation: Nurses educate patients and families to foster long-term functional independence and safe care at home. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h8)

question: Which home modification is recommended to prevent falls and protect musculoskeletal integrity?

options.A: Placing loose rugs in all hallways
options.B: Removing loose rugs and installing grab bars
options.C: Turning off lights in corridors at night
options.D: Using unstable chairs for seating

explanation: Removing loose rugs and installing grab bars in bathrooms helps prevent falls, protecting musculoskeletal health. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T1#GNS221_U1_T1_h8)

question: What is the maximum weight or age limit typically recommended for a paediatric patient to safely receive gallows traction?

options.A: Under 10 pounds or 6 months old
options.B: Under 30 pounds or generally under 2 years of age
options.C: Under 50 pounds or 5 years old
options.D: Under 75 pounds or 10 years old

explanation: Gallows traction is designed for infants and young children who weigh less than 30 pounds or are under two years of age because heavier children cannot use their own body weight safely for counter-traction. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h1)

question: In gallows traction, at what angle are the child's hips positioned relative to the body?

options.A: 30 degrees
options.B: 45 degrees
options.C: 90 degrees
options.D: 180 degrees

explanation: The technique requires the child's hips to be flexed at a ninety-degree angle to the body with the knees extended. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is the primary clinical indication for utilizing gallows traction in a paediatric patient?

options.A: Tibial plateau fracture
options.B: Femoral shaft fracture
options.C: Congenital clubfoot
options.D: Fractured clavicle

explanation: Gallows traction is primarily indicated for the management and stabilization of femoral shaft fractures in infants and toddlers. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h2)

question: Why is constant, uninterrupted traction particularly crucial for infants with femoral fractures?

options.A: Infants have slow bone healing rates
options.B: Infants have malleable bones and are prone to muscle spasms
options.C: Infants require heavy weights to stimulate growth
options.D: Infants cannot feel pain during movement

explanation: Infants have highly malleable bones and are prone to painful muscle spasms, making continuous traction essential to prevent bone overriding and ensure proper healing. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h2)

question: What type of traction is gallows traction classified as?

options.A: Skeletal traction
options.B: Skin traction
options.C: Manual traction
options.D: Balanced suspension traction

explanation: Gallows traction is a form of skin traction where pulling force is applied to the skin using adhesive or non-adhesive strips rather than pins inserted into bone. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h3)

question: What acts as the counter-weight in gallows traction?

options.A: Heavy sandbags attached to the head of the bed
options.B: The child's own upper torso and body weight
options.C: A specialized footplate bolted to the frame
options.D: Overhead pulley weights

explanation: The child's upper torso and body weight act as the counter-traction, lifting the buttocks slightly off the mattress. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h3)

question: In which direction should elastic bandages be applied when wrapping the legs for skin traction?

options.A: Proximal to distal
options.B: Distal to proximal
options.C: Circularly around the knee only
options.D: Directly over bony prominences

explanation: Bandages should be wrapped in a distal-to-proximal manner to promote venous return and ensure even pressure distribution without cutting off circulation. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h4)

question: What critical observation must the nurse make regarding the hanging weights during setup?

options.A: They must rest completely on the floor to reduce tension
options.B: They must hang freely without touching the floor or bed frame
options.C: They must be hidden from the parents' view
options.D: They must be adjusted every ten minutes

explanation: Traction weights must always hang freely and must not touch the floor or bed frame, otherwise the traction pull will be disrupted and ineffective. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h4)

question: How often should routine neurovascular checks be performed on an infant in gallows traction?

options.A: Once every 24 hours
options.B: Every shift change only
options.C: At least every 2 to 4 hours
options.D: Only when the child cries

explanation: Neurovascular assessments must be documented frequently, at least every 2 to 4 hours, to catch any signs of compromised circulation or nerve damage early. [learn more](GNS221_U1_T10#GNS221_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is a common behavioural sign of pain or distress in an infant undergoing traction?
